utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-30-PT, the Prosecutor versus Miroslav Kvocka, Milojica Kos, Mladen Radic, and Zoran Zigic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Niemann, and I appear with my colleagues Mr. Keegan and Mr. Waidyaratne, and the case manager for the Prosecutor is Ms. Reynders. Your Honours, we have moved back to here. I hope that is not inconvenient to the Court, but it does give us a bit of perspective of the bench, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Good morning, Your Honours, Mr. President. My name is Krstan Simic representing the Defence of Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Sarko Nikolic, Defence counsel for Mr. Milojica Kos, along with Ms. Jelena Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Good morning, Your Honours. I am Toma Fila and, along with Mr. Petrovic, represent the Defence of Mr. Mladjo Radic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Good morning, Your Honours. I am Attorney Simo Tosic, Defence counsel for Zoran Zigic, and I am assisted by legal counsel, Jelena Lopicic, attorney from Belgrade. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning next to the accused to make sure that they can hear in a language which they can understand. You can't. Can someone go and try get the correct channel? AN ACCUSED: We have no interpretation here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I understand there is a difficulty with the interpretation. You can now hear, can you, all of you? Very well. I just make sure that the accused can hear. That being so, this hearing has been called to deal with a number of motions. There is, firstly, a motion to amend the name of an accused and to make various other minor amendments to the indictment. We will deal with that first. That is a Prosecutor's motion, it relates to Mr. Radic, and I understand that there is no opposition to the motion. The problem is that any motion in relation to the indictment and the amendment of the indictment at this stage of the proceedings, that is, before we have started to hear evidence, must be dealt with by the confirming Judge, and it is to him or her that the Prosecution should send the motion. What we have in mind is that the motion should be sent and a transcript of this hearing, or this part of the hearing, should be sent with it, to confirm that, in fact, there is no opposition -- Mr. Fila, can I take it that that is the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) You're absolutely correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There are then a series of motions relating to the form of the amended indictment and jurisdiction, and it would seem to us convenient to deal with those motions next, hearing the Defence first and then the Prosecution can deal with all the motions together afterwards. So I shall call on the Defence. Perhaps in the order of the indictment would be most convenient. Mr. Simic, would you like to start, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence of Mr. Kvocka has filed a motion which was submitted in writing, taking into consideration that a good portion of this motion is following the same line of argument as filed by Mr. Fila regarding Article 3 and Article 1 of the Statute. I am not going to dwell on this and I will let Mr. Fila focus on that because these two motions on these particular points are practically identical. I am instead going to focus on those points which relate to the form of the indictment. I am going to try to summarise which points, and point to only those which we believe need to be highlighted. I first reaffirm all the written arguments which we have submitted, but I would like to point out that in the amended indictment, which was confirmed by the confirming Judge, my client is, for the first time, charged with responsibility pursuant to Article 7 of the Statute, and it refers to the individual criminal responsibility which has to do with planning, instigation, ordering, committing or otherwise aiding and abetting in the planning, preparation, or execution of a crime contained in Articles 225 (sic) of the present Statute. We believe that the facts stated, which are the basis for any court proceeding, and here we have in mind a number of decisions of this Tribunal, we say that the accused has the right to be given detailed information of the charges and incriminations. We believe that the minimum of this factual basis has not been provided. Nowhere has it been stated that Mr. Kvocka has ordered anyone anywhere, that he instigated anything anywhere, and we say that there are no facts in the supporting material provided by the Prosecution that Mr. Kvocka was present to a single incident which may have been a serious violation of humanitarian law. In this situation, we are unable to prepare a defence which would provide any basis for the individual criminal responsibility of Mr. Kvocka pursuant to Article 7(1). Similar arguments also apply to the charges pursuant to Article 3, which is the superior responsibility provision. We are not going to submit any arguments in that regard because we are going to point to the facts during the presentation of evidence. However, the arguments which I have just mentioned can also be referred to in point 17 of the indictment because there is no prima facie basis. The indictment does not detail the names of the guards or the members of the police force who were providing security in Omarska at that time. The indictment should have provided a sufficient factual basis, citing individuals by name, so that the responsibility of Mr. Kvocka could be contextualised. I also submit that all charges in the indictment are too vague for the Defence to be able to proceed to preparation of a defence and providing evidence which would be exculpatory. This is not to say that we are not prepared for the trial. We are prepared. But this form of indictment does not lend itself to an efficient and fair trial. In some points, the indictment is also contradictory with respect to certain facts. In almost all points, it is stated that Mr. Kvocka was in Omarska somewhere between the 26th of May and the 30th of August, 1992. However, in one of the counts of the indictment, it states that he was there between the 26th of May until about the 15th of July, and this again is contradictory and puts us in a position to have to wonder whether it has to deal with the time period of the 26th of May until the end of August or the 26th of May until the 15th of July. There are certain witness statements which clearly point that he was there for less than one month, and it is very clear that on July 1st, he was already on another duty. We believe that the Prosecution had enough elements there and, again, let me stress that the incidents which are covered in the indictment have taken place in a particular period of time and the Prosecution should have been more accurate about stating that. Further, we have points of vagueness, such as "unknown person," "unknown date," and also the Prosecution affirms that Mr. Kos and Mr. Radic were also in positions of superiority, which is not true, and if they are covering every period of time when all of them were shift commanders, that is contradictory. An attempt should have been made from a number of pieces of evidence provided by the Prosecution, a daily schedule of Mr. Kvocka should have been laid out, especially given the fact that the evidence exists that Mr. Kvocka was also working on a regular basis in the police station in Omarska. Again, these facts, had they been presented in a more detailed way, would have simplified our proceedings and contributed to judicial economy. I am not going to dwell on the cumulative responsibility which is part of Article 7(1) and 7(3), I believe that Mr. Fila will touch on that more, but the Prosecution has charged Mr. Kvocka in the alternative, which points again to a certain vagueness. Let me point out the case of the Prosecutor versus Furundzija. The Prosecution spent a lot of time trying to prove the whereabouts of Mr. Furundzija, whether he was present there or whether he was 20 metres away. In comparison, this is a very summary indictment which the Prosecution has offered in this case because there has been no attempt made to specify exactly the place where Mr. Kvocka was. We therefore ask that the Trial Chamber direct the Prosecution to clarify and specify these points of fact which we believe to be essential for the further proceeding and presentation of evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, the Defence for Mr. Kos has filed a preliminary motion to amend the indictment. The first part is a general part for an amended indictment and the second refers to concrete criminal acts. In my oral presentation, I should like to refer to the special section because I feel that to be crucial. In response to the motion, the Prosecution said that the indictment must be concise, and that is the criticism, that is to say, that the indictment as it stands is not concise, and we have a time period which is too broad, in fact, and practically encompasses the whole time of the functioning of Omarska, from the 26th of May to the 30th of August; for example, with point 5, which refers to the murders done by Kos and the other accused, but these victims are precisely defined in the case of Tadic, for example. So the Defence sees no reason why, in the case of these accused, the events which refer to these victims could not have been precisely defined in the same way as they were in the Tadic case. That is as far as this point is concerned and the other point concerning maltreatment, torture, inhumane treatment, and so on and so forth. The second thing that the Defence would like to state is that in the initial indictment, the accused Mr. Kos is accused on the basis of Article 7(3) of the Statute, but in the amended indictment, it is enlarged to encompass 7(1), and in that section too the Defence considers that criticism can be made and that the Prosecutor, in his reply, comments on this, and states that the arguments presented by the Defence were not well-placed and quotes an example. The example that the Prosecutor gives in his response is considered by the Defence to be abstract. As it is stated, it probably can exist and be explained in that way. However, the Prosecution did not throw light upon any piece of evidence from which this kind of example could be deduced and would emanate, and it is in that direction that the Defence would like to make use of the judgement in the case of the Prosecutor versus Anto Furundzija, it is para 8 of the judgement, which states that the Prosecution has been told to send a document in which it will precisely define in what way the accused has gone against Article 7(1) of the Statute, and I should like to ask that the same be done in this case and that the Defence be presented with a document which would show the responsibility of the accused's course with regard to Article 7(1) of the Statute. As far as Article 7(3) is concerned, I don't think I need give any special explanation, because it is a question of fact which will be ascertained during the trial itself. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Radic, and on behalf of the other Defence counsel as well, in keeping with Rule 72(A), under (i) and (ii), that is, challenging jurisdiction and defects in the form of the indictment, I would like to say something in that regard. The Defence was encouraged by a good idea presented by our learned colleague, Mr. Niemann, in the Dokmanovic case, that the best thing is to discuss matters of this kind before the trial begins so that we deal with facts at the trial. You have also encouraged the Defence in that respect, and I thank you for that, because I do feel that we should clarify all these questions before we begin with the concrete situation and concrete cases under the given indictment. In great detail, the Defence explained why it considers that the United Nations -- that is to say its Security Council -- did not have the intention of having Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions being placed under the competency of this Trial Chamber. And that was the first question I dealt with. The second question was that if he did not include this, as he did not, whether Common Article 3 has become part of international customary law or not, and so come under the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. As you know, in written form, I go on to explain and emphasise the difference between the Statute of this same ad hoc Tribunal for Rwanda, where after 18 months, Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions has been introduced. Then I refer to the report of the Secretary-General, and Cherif Bassiouni's opinion, and others, who said that it appears that Common Article 3 should not come under the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. It would be taking up too much of Your Honours' time if I were to expound all this again, because what I wrote, I wrote in my motion, the Prosecution provided a response, and we provided a response again, so I have nothing more to add nor any legal authority to add, nor do I have the authority to do so. But I would like to look at these questions, because they have to do with this trial and other trials, because the judgement will, of course, be used as stare decisis in other matters. I think that the criticism which has been made as regards the Tadic judgement is not a case in point, because there was a different decision made there, and this Honourable Court is not bound to the Tadic decision, particularly because the stare decisis principle is not always applied in international law as it is in national jurisdictions, and for that reason the Tadic judgement does not represent a judgement that can be applied in this case. The Defence also looked at Article 1 of the Statute and considered that particular article. We also consider that this high and distinguished Court cannot deal with all matters at once, and at all times, and that precisely for that reason it states that the competence of this International Tribunal is a serious violation of humanitarian law, and I say this in all seriousness. What we say with regard to Witness F cannot be considered a serious violation of international humanitarian law, even if it did occur as it occurred, and that would be below the competencies of this International Tribunal. That kind of question will come up on the agenda of national courts in Bosnia-Herzegovina when they are established and when they are capacitated to deal with cases of that kind. Furthermore, the Defence looked at Point B, and the challenges in the form of the indictment and their defects. I have already expounded this in writing, and referred to three particular decisions with regard to the defects in the form of the indictment. I would like to quote them, and then I won't be taking up more of your valuable time, Your Honours. One of the decisions, in the case of Dusko Tadic, the 14th of November, 1995, as a response to the Defence motion with regard to the form of the indictment. The second decision is in the Tihomir Blaskic case, and a decision there, once again, a response to criticisms as to precision, and the third and latest decision was one taken with regard to the Milorad Krnojelac case. I don't know at the moment -- that is, we filed our motion after the term given by Your Honours for one simple reason, and that is because the decision was taken after that time limit, that deadline. I don't know if it was distributed; I have no knowledge on that matter. But we did send it out as soon as we had received it, and it is the decision of the 24th of February of this year, where we adopt the criticism made by the Defence and which states to the Prosecution that it should precisely define when the actual crime took place and who it refers to. The last thing that I have to say in this sense is that we have been using too much descriptive terms, that the Prosecution is using descriptive terms and bringing itself into a collision of a certain kind. I would like to state the introduction of the indictment with Mladjo Radic where he says he was responsible for everything that took place in the camp when Dzelko Meakic was not there, Miloslav Kvocka was not there, and civilians and inspectors, they're all referred to, and when that was within his shift. We never know, according to the indictment, when it actually took place; that is to say when Meakic, Kvocka, and these civilians and inspectors were not there and when those shifts actually took place, what particular day. So it is no problem that the learned Prosecution, via its multitude of inspectors that it has, to send them to the Omarska police station, where documentation exists as to the schedule of the individual shifts, because with us, during Tito's Yugoslavia, at least, there was some order, and we would keep documents of this kind for 20 years at least. Perhaps the Prosecution has evidence of this kind, but it doesn't agree with the Prosecution to put them forward, because then they would have to specify what day each one of the individuals had a shift and what happened during those shifts, and that Meakic and Kvocka, all the investigators, all the civilians, were in fact not present. Only then would we have command responsibility of Mladjo Radic, had he been the shift commander, which it is asserted that he was, and which he was not. So without precisely defined facts of this kind, we're going to sink into a sea of various proceedings and will never emerge. That is all I have to say. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, the Defence of Zoran Zigic would like to stress that we fully remain with the stand taken with our preliminary response to the motion and to stress that everything that my colleagues have said with regard to the precisions of the indictment I consider to stand. The place, the time, when the acts occurred, were not precisely defined, and so we should like to associate ourselves with them. In our motion we stressed and said that we have severance of responsibility in the indictment, and the fact that there was a change in the Rules, particularly with regard to Rule 82(B), and that the accused that I represent is not responsible for command responsibilities, not held responsible for command responsibilities. So that in that sense I don't think it would be economical to have one single trial, and in particular I should like to highlight the provision of Rule 94(B). In view of the Rules and provisions, I feel that there could be conflicting interests, bearing in mind the defence of the accused and also that this could harm the accused. All this I say in the aim of having a fair and expeditious trial. As far as that proposal is concerned, I think that at all events the Trial Chamber should once again look into the matter, because all indications point to the fact that the accused that I represent is not there to answer for command responsibility. So in order to have a fair and expeditious trial, I think that there should be a severance in the trial proceedings. Thank you so much. Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning. I shall endeavour not to repeat anything already submitted by the Prosecution, but rather refer to some general points, some of the issues raised this morning, and then to the extent that I can assist Your Honours with any question that you may have based on the submissions. Dealing first with the issue of the jurisdiction, to remove that, since it was raised only briefly this morning, we would stand essentially on our pleadings, Your Honour. It doesn't appear that anything new has been raised this morning. The essential points we believe are of most relevance are the fact that, of course, the concept of stare decisis is, and should be, applicable before this Tribunal for it to function effectively. We would note specifically that the issue of stare decisis appears to have been considered and utilised in the decision in the Krnojelac case referred to today, and I would point specifically to paragraph 5 of that decision. In particular, with respect to the claims made by the accused here, and in particular Mr. Fila in his briefs, as we indicate in our response, the claims made by these accused are the very same claims that have been litigated previously, and in particular decided by the Appeals Chamber on this issue on those very specific arguments. They have been redressed a bit, but they are in effect the same arguments, and therefore we believe that the prior determination of this Tribunal should stand. With respect to the form of the indictment, we would respectfully suggest that when considering the concept of the particularity that's required in the pleading of a case, it must be considered contextually. It is clear that the nature of an indictment for a particular actor in a single crime will by definition be a more specific pleading. As one moves away from the concept of a specific crime -- a one-off event, if you will -- and you move away from criminal liability based on direct commission of an act, the very nature of the pleading itself changes, and the particularity which is necessary changes. We would in fact agree with the citation in the Krnojelac case, the citation coming in paragraph 14 to the case of RV Associated Northern Collieries, where the Court said that; "the opposite party here, the accused, shall be placed in possession of its broad outlines and the constituted facts which are said to raise his legal liability. He is to receive sufficient information to ensure a fair trial and to guard against what the law terms 'surprise,' but he is not entitled to be told the mode by which the case is to be proved against him." That quote will obviously have very different meanings in different contexts and in different types of cases. The standard under the Statute and the Rules calls for a concise statement of the facts. "Concise", of course, meaning "summary"; not necessarily specific in the nature of the detail requested by accused in their present motions. In fact, to give the accused the detail which they are seeking, one would not have a concise statement of the facts; one would have an extensive and lengthy statement of facts. The question is whether the accused have been placed on notice of the material facts which give rise to their criminal responsibility. That is, of course, as stated in the Krnojelac case, the particular acts of the accused or the particular course of conduct on his part which are alleged to constitute that responsibility. The crimes charged against these accused are all course-of-conduct violations, and with respect to the persecution charge, in fact entail essentially an allegation of common purpose. With the exception of the accused Zigic, these are not cases of individual specific one-off crimes but rather a series of criminal acts committed by these accused, or at their direction, and not the type of pleadings which the Defence have referred to in other judgements before this Tribunal; for example, the Furundzija case. That was in essence a one-event indictment. Similarly, the Tadic case, Mr. Tadic was charged with specific acts in addition to the overall crime of persecution. Therein the pleadings, and as accepted by the Trial Chamber in the decision on the form of the indictment, reflected different standards, in essence, in the pleadings. We believe that those different standards are reflected in this indictment when one views the allegations as alleged, how they are in fact drafted against the three accused charged with criminal responsibility by virtue of their positions as superiors in addition to their individual responsibility, and that of Mr. Zigic, who is charged on a number of occasions with specific crimes in addition to the overall persecution count. With respect to the persecution count, the pleadings are the same as the other three accused. With respect to the particular crimes, there are specific victims, dates, and places alleged. So the Prosecution believes that the pleadings do meet the requirements of the Statute and the Rules given the context of the nature of the responsibility and the crimes for which the accused are charged. For example, with respect to Mr. Kvocka, the complaint is that the allegations are too vague, yet the accused entered pleas, and in fact, as his counsel indicated today, they are prepared to go to trial. That in effect is an inconsistent position, one which the Prosecution believes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Keegan, I don't know that that's a very good point. They pleaded to the material that was available, and they say they're ready for trial. But even if you're right about the nature of the pleadings in this Tribunal, and that detailed pleadings are not required, even if you're right about that, there will come a time when the Prosecution must clearly spell out how it is said, in the case of each accused, that he is guilty of these offences, what it is that he said or did that makes him guilty according to you. While you may be right, of course, that the mode by which the Prosecution are going to prove the case -- i.e. the way they're going to prove it -- does not have to appear in the pleading. In due course, it must be made plain to the Trial Chamber, and of course to the defendants, how it is alleged that each one of them committed each offence. No doubt, with your experience, you have that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I may respond to that, we believe that in fact the achievement of that requirement -- that is, to make it plain to both the accused and to the Trial Chamber of the actual basis of the accused's responsibility, those come in two different stages, of course. As reflected in the prior decisions and the most recent one, the Krnojelac -- and I keep butchering that name; I apologise -- case, there is in effect a balance between the form, the pleading of the indictment itself and the content of the supporting material. While decisions make clear that the supporting material cannot take the place of the indictment, cannot make up for substantial defects, the indictment must be read in the context, as I indicated, of the crimes and of the supporting material. The issue for the accused is whether the indictment meets the requirements of the Statute and the Rules, which are of course reflective of the international standards as reflected in the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, to give him notice of the charges against him. The second aspect, in terms of preparation for a defence, that must be considered not only on the face of the indictment but also in the context of the supporting material provided to the accused. I believe that has been accepted in these decisions that have been referred to before this Tribunal, and they're certainly accepted in the case law flowing from the European Court of Human Rights, based upon the European Convention of Human Rights and the ICCPR. With respect to when that must be made plain to the Trial Chamber, we believe, in the first instance, that comes with, under our practice, the submissions of the Pre-Trial brief to the Trial Chamber, at which point the Prosecution has generally been charged by chambers, in my experience, to provide the detail of the case upon which it intends to rely, in essence providing a roadmap for the Trial Chamber. Opening statements provide the second aspect of that notice to the Trial Chamber, and the third and most important component is of course the actual trial itself, so that -- yes, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but there's a distinction there. You refer to the detail which will be provided in the Pre-Trial brief. It is of course not only the detail, some of which has been referred to this morning; it's also the Prosecution case. I believe in United States practice it's referred to as the theory, sometimes; that's not a particular concept I'm familiar with, but I think I understand what's meant. We would rather say the Prosecution case, how is it that the Prosecution propose to prove in each case that the accused is guilty of the particular offence? That is what the Trial Chamber wants to know, and that's what the accused are entitled to know. How is it said by the Prosecution that they are guilty? That needs to be said at the outset. Of course, during the course of the case, as the evidence is given, it may be necessary to change positions, because the evidence may vary, and you can never tell at the outset precisely what's going to be proved and what isn't. But at least at the beginning, the Court and the Defence should know how it is being alleged, how it is being said, that the Prosecution are going to prove the case against all the defendants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We believe, for example, in the present indictment, a distinction between this indictment, for example, and the Krnojelac case. In the decision, the Trial Chamber refers to the fact that in the background section of that indictment, there was information which was of relevance to the issues being complained of, but that that information was background only and didn't address, because it was not part of the actual pleadings -- the charges, that is -- did not address the concerns. In this case, for example, we have specifically stated that that background section is incorporated and re-alleged for each of the particular charges. That background section, we believe, provides the underlying basis for the charges, and particularly the Article 5 charges, but also substantiates the underlying requirement for Article 3 as well. That background section, when read in conjunction with the paragraphs alleging the superior authority liability, the basis for it, and then with the particular crimes alleged, if read together, we believe does provide exactly the theory of the Prosecution case: That these accused, with respect to the persecution count, all participated in an ongoing, systematic, and widespread attack on the civilian population within the Opstina Prijedor; that these accused played a particular role with respect to giving effect to that persecution in the conduct of the camps. That's why, with respect to some of the particular complaints made, there is no merit in the complaint that the three accused charged under superior responsibility have no relation to the Keraterm and Trnopolje camps because, in fact, of course those other camps formed a part of the overall campaign of persecution, Omarska being one of the camps, but one of the three which was being utilised. There was of course a relationship between those three camps as indicated in the proceedings and in the supporting material. With respect to the fourth accused, Zigic, his role in that persecution was slightly different in that he was a tool of the leadership as opposed to part of that leadership which the other three accused were. The complaint about superior authority, that the specificity of dates and times not being reflected in the indictment we believe are not appropriate because it is the entire period of the operation of the camp that is the relevant time frame. In this case, it amounts to less than 90 days as opposed to the 16 months or so alleged generally in the Krnojelac case. So the objection there as to the time specificity we think is addressed because we have a much more narrow focus of time, and the particular places are alleged because the conduct occurred in the camps. To say that the accused Radic or Kos had no authority when the accused Kvocka or the camp commander Meakic were present is a legally untenable argument. Their authority may be superseded by their superiors but it does not derogate their authority to their subordinates. They still have authority over their subordinates whether the commander is in the camp or not. To follow that line of argument would indicate that only the commanding generals of armies could be held responsible and not the field commander whose troops are actually committing the crime. That, of course, is an untenable position under international law with respect to command responsibility. So we believe that, again, under the context of these crimes, when the entire document is read together, those concerns are addressed because the entire document is incorporated into each of the particular charges. In addition, the accused then have reference to the supporting material, and in the supporting material there is reference to particular crimes and dates that aren't mentioned in the indictment itself, although some of those crimes are mentioned because, with respect to the allegations against the accused Zigic, to the extent those crimes are committed in Omarska, they're directly relevant to the three accused. To the extent they were committed in Trnopolje or Keraterm or even out in town, they are still relevant to these accused to the extent that those acts by the accused Zigic reflect part of the operation of the persecution. So to the extent that the other acts of Zigic which did not occur in Omarska fall within the persecution, they are also relevant then to these accused as evidence of the ongoing persecution. I would like to address also, Your Honour, the issue raised by Mr. Fila with respect to the crimes against Witness F and that they don't rise to the level required to reach this Tribunal, that is, serious violations of international law. It would be perhaps possible if an accused was able to sever each particular act of which he is accused to make that same argument. It is a rather untenable argument when any one particular act is considered in the framework of a course of criminal conduct, and that is the nature by which those charges are brought. They are representative of the course of conduct which was ongoing, and the fact that that crime may be relevant to establishing the crime of persecution which, of course, falls squarely within a serious violation of international humanitarian law, and, in and of itself, amounts to a violation within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal, it is entirely appropriate for that charge to be brought before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, arising from what you have said. You referred to Krnojelac. That also, as I recollect, is a case involving a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You say the distinction between that case and this one is that the events there were spread over a much longer period. Sixteen months, I think you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe the allegation there was April '92 to August '93, and I intended to make mention of particular aspects of that decision which are similar to the complaints made by the accused here with respect to specificity, and in particular, I would note again that the Trial Chamber itself in that case found that the background section answered some of the issues but, because it had not been incorporated into the charges, could not be considered to address those issues with respect to the charges. Here that's exactly the opposite case. You will find in the indictment that they are specifically re-alleged and incorporated. I believe it is paragraph 18. Yes, paragraph 18 re-alleges and incorporates into each of the charges the background section. With respect to the time frame, we believe that there is a substantial distinction between alleging a relevant time frame that amounts to somewhat less than 90 days and one that amounts to 16 to 18 months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The other matter I was going to raise with you are some specific points which were made by Defence counsel. In the case of Mr. Simic, he says that there were contradictory dates alleged against Mr. Kvocka when he was at the camp, and Mr. Fila raised the question of whether you had the lists of shifts. Now, that, of course, is a detail matter, but there may be no harm in raising it now because, he says, that would throw much light on these allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As to the first allegation, the distinction between the dates used for Mr. Kvocka relate to the distinction between the persecution count overall and particular crimes because the evidence does, in fact, indicate, in the main, that Mr. Kvocka left the camp sometime between the 1st of July and mid July. There is, however, information that he returned to the camp at the end, and it is based on those contingencies of proof which you alluded to earlier, Your Honour, that those relevant time frames are pled. Now, to the extent that obviously the evidence at trial would indicate that he left in mid July and never returned, then, of course, any acts which came after that would not be relevant to the issue of his criminal responsibility in terms of finding him guilty or responsible for those crimes. They could, theoretically, be relevant to issues of intent, motive, whether it was widespread and systematic, so there is still relevance to the acts potentially against him even after the fact, but they could not obviously be used with respect to his particular findings of criminal responsibility. So that is the basis for those dates as alleged that way. With respect to this issue of schedules, clearly, Your Honour, those would be relevant evidence if they exist and certainly if the Prosecution ever is in possession of them. That's a separate matter, however, from whether or not the accused has sufficient notice for purposes of his case, and we believe that, obviously, that kind of schedule is not necessary to provide the notice required for an indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, I accept that entirely. It is merely that the issue, having been raised, I wanted to pursue it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: There was one other aspect, Your Honour, I would raise, and that was the question, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you do, may I take it you don't have those lists or schedules?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, we do not have those schedules, as far as we're aware. As we have made reference before, Your Honour, of course, we are still continuing the review of the document collections. We are limited by resources and we are working as quickly as we can. As far as we're aware, having gone through virtually all the documents, they don't exist, and as I understand, based on my information from the Defence, they indicate those records would be specifically held in the Omarska police station. Well, we have not been to the Omarska police station, so we would certainly not have the particular records they're referring to. Now, to the extent they may have been in the Prijedor police station, we may have documents, but not that we are aware of. The final point that I wanted to refer to was the issue raised by Mr. Tosic about the -- I'm sorry, it was actually made by Mr. Fila, raised with respect to the issue of the identification of the specific perpetrators and of the victims with respect to command responsibility. I would note that the decision he refers to, the Krnojelac case, indicates that the categories, if particular names are not known, that the categories of the perpetrators and the victims is sufficient. In that case, the problem was, it was unclear whether, with respect to the allegations relating to the superior authority of the accused in that case, the perpetrators were actually guards under his control or not. Here the pleadings do specifically indicate that the crimes were committed either by guards or by visitors to the camp who were allowed in to commit crimes but were under the direct control of the various accused. Similarly with the victims, it's clear from the pleadings that the victims are all Bosnian Muslims or Bosnian Croats who were prisoners in the camp, or the various camps in the case of Mr. Zigic. So we believe that the specificity required by the Trial Chamber in Krnojelac is met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. The one other issue raised was the severance issue. To the extent that there are any questions, we believe, obviously, our pleadings are sufficient. I would only note that today in the pleadings there is no basis for the severance indicated clearly. Here, counsel for Mr. Zigic raised the issue of conflicting interests under Rule 82 but doesn't provide a basis or elaborate what the conflicting interests are except to say the general assertion that Mr. Zigic isn't charged under Article 7(3). Whether we believe that the Defence has not raised any of the bases reflected under Article 82 and that the main issue here, of course, as it is in any severance motion, is a question of prejudice, the accused here failed to make a showing of prejudice to the accused, there is no conflict of interest with respect to the charges, rather the interests of justice, both with respect to speedy trial for all accused here as well as the interests of justice with respect to the Prosecution evidence and particularly the witnesses necessary to prove these crimes, would indicate that a joint trial is the most appropriate forum for these four accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now I turn to the Defence. Would anybody like to respond? In the same order then, please. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, I would like to go back to the jurisdiction regarding Common Article 3 and whether it has been incorporated or not in the provisions. At one point, Mr. Keegan said that the Defence had offered no new arguments which would open the possibility of re-examination of this decision. I would like to point out -- perhaps I did not read or follow well -- but in the Secretary-General's report, in paragraphs 41, 42, 43, the basis for Common Article 3 is introduced, and there it is specifically stated that the legal basis for this provision was The Hague Conventions, Conventions 3 and 4. At another point in this report, it is mentioned that the Hague Conventions are not in contradiction with the Geneva Conventions. My understanding of it was that the Secretary-General's position was justified by the fact that there was no contradiction between these provisions, but I think he drew a clear line that the legal basis for the relation was to provide the basis for the humanisation of the armed conflict itself, so my thinking is that the drafting of this provision would be focused on the armed conflict itself and that this Article would only apply to those provisions. In the Secretary-General's report, paragraphs 41, 42, 43 lead me to believe that we can construe this, so I would like to have that point taken into consideration when you reach your decision. Now, something with respect to the defects in the form of the indictment. Mr. Keegan avers that it refers to all four of the accused and it was a systematic persecution of non-Serbs in the Prijedor municipality. We believe that we should take into account the status of these accused. Mr. Kvocka is just a regular police officer, before the war, during, and after the war, even to date, that is, until he was arrested, he was a policeman. Mr. Kos was a waiter. He was mobilised during the war. Today we learn that they were part of a system of planned persecution of non-Serbs because, by applying the laws and rules of the former Yugoslavia which were adopted by Bosnia and Herzegovina in this terrible war, they became part of a machine, became part of a system such as was set up in Omarska, Keraterm, Trnopolje, and so on. Again, in response to Mr. Keegan's arguments, we say that the indictment does not provide the factual basis which would place our clients into the context which is alleged here, that they have consciously taken part in the systematic military system of persecution. There are documents which talk about the setup of the investigating centre of Omarska. The police station in Omarska was to provide security. I don't know if somebody who is part of a security agency and goes to work there, based on these provisions that were set up, makes him part of the systematic persecution. When talking about the command responsibility or superior responsibility, it has to be individualised because a superior person has to be responsible or liable for specific persons. Mr. Kvocka cannot be charged with anything and everything that happened in the Prijedor area, he cannot be made responsible for the Keraterm camp as well, the events which took place there, and I come from that area. We would be able to provide many more facts to provide a more specific context for indictments. Also, the way the indictment is framed precludes the possibility of alibi because it charges all of the accused being everywhere at all times. If they had shifts even of 12 hours, I cannot see how you can accuse them of being there for 24 hours at a time. So the argument of the Prosecution, that they were part of a premeditated system and plan, that they were part of a plan which they have adopted and carried out as their own systematically, has to be supported by a much broader basis in fact. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I would like to ask you a question in relation to the reach of Article 3 of the Statute. What the Prosecutor is saying is that the very points that you have raised in relation to that Article were specifically considered by the Appellate Chamber in the Tadic case. There are three main points: First, whether Common Article 3 is included in Article 3, whether Common Article 3 is part of customary international law, and whether Common Article 3 entails individual criminal responsibility. All those points were explicitly considered by the Appellate Chamber in the Tadic case. You are now asking a Trial Chamber to reconsider these points which were determined as a matter of law by the Appellate Chamber. Is it not a prescription for chaos if each Trial Chamber had the option, had the right, to review decisions of the Appellate Chamber on questions of law, and what would be the point of the Statute establishing an Appellate Chamber with specific power to correct mistakes of law and mistakes of fact if, having issued its decisions, those decisions are not binding on Appellate Chambers? Would you like to comment on that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, the arguments you raise are indeed convincing. However, the Defence also views this Tribunal as something new. We are all brought into the situation of implementing certain rules that have just been adopted several years ago, and I believe that both my colleague Mr. Fila and I have provided arguments to the effect that this, being a new decision, it still needs to be tested. We were also looking at the Rwanda Tribunal. I have to say that we are not fully convinced that the arguments provided are fully convincing. We think that we are still at a stage where we need to re-examine things and readdress, and I don't think that it would lead to judicial chaos. I think that there are enough arguments which I find lead to the overturning of the Tadic decision yet. We therefore believe that this position needed further re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but if it is to be overturned, then it has to be overturned by the Appellate Chamber itself. It can't be overturned by the Trial Chamber. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I accept that argument too, and if our motion is not granted, we will obviously turn to the Appellate Chamber in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) In my motion, I did not touch upon Article 3, so I will spare you the chaos there, but I have additional arguments. I believe that there is a certain chaos emanating from the indictment referring charges relating to Mr. Kos. I may have missed something due to the interpretation, but I think that we really need to specify the time frame of the crimes for which the accused is charged as a perpetrator, and I raise the very Tadic case as a basis for that. Now, this is one point. The second point that I just heard for the first time is that the accused Kos supported what Mr. Zigic did in Keraterm and Trnopolje in the original indictment. Again, I don't know whether this was interpreted correctly to me, but this is what I heard. In the original indictment, there is no Trnopolje and Keraterm, but now the way the Prosecutor said we should understand the indictment, I somehow construe that Kos should also be liable for what happened in Keraterm or Trnopolje, and in no point, nowhere in the indictment, is the presence of Kos mentioned because he never was there -- excuse me. Trnopolje and Keraterm; he was never there. As far as Mr. Zigic is concerned -- and this is something that will be argued in the presentation of evidence -- he never knew this man. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Nikolic, and this will be spelled out by the Prosecution -- it is not for me to do their job at all -- but they say, presumably, that the fact that a person wasn't at a particular place or didn't know another particular person is neither here nor there if they were part of a general enterprise, a joint enterprise, which involved the particular crime which is alleged. So they may well be saying that it doesn't matter where a particular person was at a time. If he was part in some way of the persecution, then he is guilty. But no doubt that is a matter which can be followed in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honour, if we stipulate that Mr. Kos was in Omarska, we can do that right away, but here he is also charged with some specific things, and in this way, the alibi defence is precluded because the indictment charges that there were three shifts, and they are indicted as shift commanders. One is here in The Hague and the others are at large. Now, the alibi defence is precluded by this. In the supporting material that the Prosecution provided, I cannot believe that there is something in the supporting materials -- the additional supporting material that has now been provided to the Defence where this is stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) First of all, I would like to refer to the question of Judge Robinson, that is to say, whether there would be legal chaos if the decisions of the Appeals Chamber were not abided by. If the decision of a Trial Chamber is erroneous and if new facts emerge which would lead to another judgement of the Appeals Chamber had those circumstances been known, then the whole case can be brought before the court again, and we would seek that that be done. I think that that is included in everybody's national right. The problem is that the Rules do not provide for an institution of that kind and, second, the fact that Tadic, who was tried and is being tried, would be interested in bringing the case back to trial and not us. For example, in the Celebici case, the Defence, once again, asked for the re-opening of the case by the Appeals Chamber because there is no way that we can indicate the elements which were not present or not in evidence during the case and when the Trial Chamber made its judgement. Second, if I understood my learned colleague Mr. Keegan properly, he said that the time will come when he will precisely define the indictment, and that leads me to conclude that he himself agrees that the indictment is not sufficiently precise. The problem that is raised now is when am I going to wait for that time and what can I do after that time when the Prosecution has decided that the right time has come for him to define more precisely the time span? So it is not up to the Court to keep people with this lack of knowledge and that they should not receive something had they had a clear idea of what they were actually being accused of. So the Court cannot resort to ruse but to justice and truth, and that is where the specific features of the Prosecution in this Tribunal, compared to national prosecutions, lie. I therefore consider that a fair trial would be possible only if the accused knows in precise detail what he is being accused of, what he is being charged of, and when these acts were committed. So it is not a problem when we say the name and surname of the individual, if we say that it is Omarska and that something happened there. In the same way, you can say that the term "Muslim" represents equality which is sought for in canulae. One Muslim, a particular Muslim man; what does that mean? It is just a religious denomination. It doesn't say when, doesn't say why. It is not a category. That is what my learned friend Mr. Keegan was talking about. He does not refer to the situation with regard to Witness F. I said that Witness F was twice accused of the same thing, and you have this in writing in point 17, I believe, and 27 -- Count 17 and Count 27. Mr. Keegan does not refer to that, and this was raised twice in the two counts. The third matter that I wanted to draw your attention to was that in the general premises of the indictment, Counts 19, 20, 21, and 22 -- for example, when any of the accused are being mentioned, let us take Milojica Kos, for example, or Mladjo Radic, and it is stated that he was the leader of the shift, and that when he was present in the camp, he was in a superior position with regard to the other personnel in the camp, which means that when he was present in the camp, for the Prosecution and for us, it means something, when he was present in the camp means something. And argumentum a contrario. It states that when he was not present, he was not responsible. So how are we going to ascertain, if the indictment is imprecise, when he was present and when not? If the indictment refers to events that took place in 1992 and was written in 1994, is it perhaps a lack of seriousness that we have not found time in five years in the entire Tadic case to go to the police station in Omarska and get the documents from it? When the protector of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Westendorp, is able to replace presidents and states and do what they like, can they not go to the police station in Omarska, for the Prosecutor to get that documentation so that we can ascertain when Milojica Kos was there, when the accused were there, when Mladjo Radic was there and what were they when they were there. So in each of these statements that we have dating back to the Tadic trial, the victims say that it was the policemen, the victims say that they were the policemen of the police station in Omarska when these three people are in question, that is, two of them, two of the accused. Is it not a good idea to look at the documents of the police station in Omarska? Were they policemen? When were they on duty? What were they doing while they were on duty? We can't wait for the right time for Mr. Keegan to decide when he is going to do that. Those documents exist. I have seen the list, but I cannot get them because I am not the Prosecutor nor am I Westendorp, and I am not even a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina to boot. You have the power to ask for those documents. You have them proprio moto, if the Prosecution wishes to do so -- that is, does not want to do so. My request is that if the Prosecution does not wish to do so, that it should be made to do so, so that we can see who was in which shift and what happened in a particular shift, and individuals must have names and surnames and not just give a general category and say "a Muslim," I don't know any category like that. That is a religious denomination. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, with full respect for Mr. Keegan, I should like to refer to what he said in connection to my defendant and the positions in the indictment that it is not essential, as regards the details, when concrete actions took place, and I should like to stress in that regard that in the entire indictment and case, the Prosecution does not have facts as to when my defendant was in the reserve formation of the police force and when he was recruit, and also it is unacceptable what Mr. Keegan said with regard to the operation of persecution and that my defendant was sort of the extended arm of the leadership. If we look at the status of my defendant, my defendant was not a leader, nor was he a member of any party, nor did he take part in any civilian authorities, and the question can be raised whether this kind of indictment can say that he took part in a persecution. As regards the stand that there is no grounds for severance, I should like to stress that two-thirds of the evidence and material that we are going to present during the case will refer to command responsibility, which has nothing to do with my defendant, so that for that period and the evidence, my defendant could not even be in the courtroom, outside the courtroom, because all the witnesses with regard to the other accused refer to command responsibility, so that they have nothing to do with my own accused, and I thought that because of a fair and expeditious trial, there should be severance in this case. Thank you so much from me. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Bennouna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I would like to ask the Defence a question after the presentation made by Mr. Fila and also the position stated by Mr. Tosic on the question of precision. I am tempted to ask what that means. If I understand correctly, there is a question of dates. That is the first issue that was raised: There is the question of dates. One must also specify exactly what dates we are referring to and when the dates with which the accused are charged took place and also the presence of such and such an accused in the camps. I believe that the Prosecutor did not deny the fact -- everybody is referring back to Krnojelac, the decision that was rendered, in one way or another, and what we know here of this decision is that they stated that there was the possibility of having additional precision on the part of the Prosecution. We should also define what this mean. What does the term "precision" mean? Once we have a better idea of what "precision" means, we will be in a better position to make a ruling on this matter. The other issue is whether or not the accused were present in the camp, as I stated, and the other question which was asked, if I understood Mr. Fila correctly, is whether the responsibility is based on their presence in the camp. That is a question of law; it is no longer a question of fact. One can be responsible even if one is not present, of course. The other question of fact -- I am trying now to follow what you are requesting in what you stated -- that when there is command responsibility at issue, then one must specify also what crimes were committed by the subordinates, Article 7(3), that is to say, to establish the link between the commander and his subordinates, and it is specified quite clearly in our Statute, I believe. It states that if the superior knew, or had reason to know and also punish him if he did not take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or to punish. So these are the matters before us now. I would like to hear from you whether or not there are any questions of fact that you would like to ask and to be as clear as possible with regards to the indictment and also have the Prosecutor's position on specific matters because it was stated that the Prosecutor, the Office of the Prosecutor, in his pre-trial motion, he states that he was prepared to set forth additional precisions, and you stated that that was a question of strategy. Why doesn't he present them now and not later? Of course, there is no ruse here. It is simply a matter of working with transparency, total transparency, and for everyone to have as fair a trial as possible. So if there are any precisions that may be made available, then perhaps they will be given without any further ado, further delay. From what I have understood of your position, can you state whether there are matters that could be specified in relation to this indictment in reference to what I have just stated, and, if so, can we then turn to the Prosecution and see whether they have these precisions in hand at this time, and, if so, can they then respond immediately to your request?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, for you to be able to understand me clearly and briefly, the basis of my criticism of the indictment is the indictment itself, and I quoted the fact that the accused were accused as shift commanders, which they deny in their defence. But let us take it that they were shift commanders. According to Article 7(3), they are held responsible only if them and their subordinates were in the camp. That is what it says in the indictment, "when he was present in the camp." So to define more precisely the indictment is something the Defence requires because I want to know the dates -- I apologise. Let's begin again. The camp lasted for less than 90 days. It is not contested -- and Mr. Keegan knows this full well -- that they had shifts: one shift for 12 hours and then it would not work for 24 hours, which means that each of them, according to that rotation principle, 12, 48, 24, he was not there for at least 30 days of the 90 days that the camp existed, according to that principle. Or 60 -- or he wasn't there 60 days. That is to say, he was not there a third of the time. Quite simply, he was not there for a third of the time. Yes, sorry. One-third of the time he worked, two-thirds of the time they were not there and didn't work, which means that each of the accused of that rank will be held responsible only for 30 days and not for the other 60 days, and that is the reason why I am asking that via the police station we ascertain what days were in point, and when the shifts worked, and what happened while that shift was on duty, and if we ascertain that Mladjo Radic was indeed the shift commander, then he will be held responsible according to 7(1) of the Statute for when he and his shift were on duty because that is what he is being accused of, whereas I cannot prepare a defence for the other 60 days because that is not something that I would have to deal with, it is not a matter of interest to me, and that is the precision that I seek. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, you have raised this question of the shift documents. We take the view that this is purely a matter of evidence; it doesn't affect the form of the indictment. We take your point that these are crucial documents, if they are available, and would be very important for a trial. After this hearing, when we have heard all the motions, we shall have a Status Conference, and it may be possible then to pursue matters further with the Prosecution as to the availability or the possibility of obtaining those documents. That might be the appropriate time to deal with these.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Your Honours. I would just like to give the other half of my answer to the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) One limitation we spoke about were shifts. The second limitation, which the Prosecution goes on to state in its description and says that Mladjo Radic and Kos were in a superior position with regard to the overall personnel in the camp, and that's okay, but the problem arises after that, "except for the commander and deputy commander and most of the visitors." If we ascertain when the shifts were, that is to say, when they worked, and that is a question of fact which I agree with, it is also a question of fact when they were not in the camp and when, during their shift, the commander -- when the commander, deputy commanders, and most of the visitors were not in the camp because if the commander, the deputy commander, and most of the visitors were there, once again, argumento tempere criminis, Meakic, the commander was present, so we are not responsible. So we have to know, once again, more precise details, when it happened -- when all this did not happen, that is to say, and then -- and I would like this to be my last sentence -- what happened at that particular time? Because we have ascertained theoretically the command responsibility, 7(3) when Meakic wasn't there, when the visitors weren't there and when the deputy commander was not there, but it remains to be seen what happened next, and that is the important part, because if I were to have command responsibility, some crime must have been committed, and that is not included here, and that is another question that we have to settle. Before I begin to collect my evidence to ascertain whether the actual things happened then or did not happen then, and that is why I protested when the category was used, saying "a Muslim." That is not a legal category, "a Muslim," it once happened that he was beaten, killed, or whatever. When? When? And then I can see who was responsible for that. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is time for the usual break. We will sit again at ten past twelve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will consider the motions which were discussed this morning, and we will give our decisions in due course in writing. I turn next to the remaining motions, which I hope we can get through by the luncheon adjournment. I would also like, if it's possible, to hold a Status Conference after we've heard the motions, again this morning, to review the current state of the trial. The remaining motions which I have here are first of all a Prosecutor's motion -- they're all Prosecutor's motions. There's one for judicial notice of adjudicated facts. There is another relating to the admission of documentary evidence, and finally there is a request for the admission of the evidence of an expert. It may be that we can take these matters in that order, beginning with the motion for judicial notice, which we have, and the response from the Defence, we have. If I have understood it aright, the Prosecutor is asking for some 583 items to be the subject of judicial notice. Those all arise from the Celebici and Tadic judgements. As far as the Defence are concerned, the Defence of Mr. Kvocka accepts none; that of the remaining defendants would accept Items 1 to 125, and I'm referring now to the annex to the Prosecutor's motion which sets out these items, items 1 to 125, relating to the context of the conflict, and the background, except for 17 which are spelt out in the Defence, so that we can understand the background. Is that the position in relation to the defendants? Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, first of all, I would like to express dissatisfaction because the materials which were the basis for this motion have not been provided to me by the Prosecution, but taking into consideration my desire that the Trial Chamber proceed to the trial as soon as possible, I have given my statement referring to the Rules of Procedure. However, I stated some facts could be adjudicated which I find to be incontrovertible, and I would now like to enumerate those, but again, let me point out that I did not receive all the materials. The Kvocka Defence agrees to accept 1 through 6, 8, 10 to 17, 21 to 70, 74, 78 to 87, 89, 96 to 113, 113 to 125. So we join the positions of Mr. Fila and Mr. Nikolic, who have also agreed to stipulating these facts as adjudicated. We are also prepared to accept them because they are just incontrovertible in themselves, rather than that they are any product of the trials. But we again would like to point out that we need to receive the materials which the Prosecution has used to base these adjudicated facts on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, so that I have that, you adopt the same position as the remaining Defence counsel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That being the position, I turn to the Prosecution. Mr. Niemann, if you would like to add anything to what you said, as briefly as possible, please; I think we've got the arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It seems that there is a considerable portion on which agreement is being reached on. It really then becomes a matter for the Chamber to decide whether or not you consider that any of the other material should be judicially noticed in accordance with Rule 94(B). I don't wish to add anything further in terms of submissions; I just wish to point out a couple of matters which have been raised by the Defence. Firstly, they have said that the materials that we have referred to from the Tadic case are the subject of an appeal; they are not in fact the subject of an appeal for at least the vast majority of them. There are perhaps the incidents to which the name of Mr. Tadic has been referred to concerning his particular crimes; that could be resolved, not the incidents themselves, but his involvement in it has been appealed. If Your Honours had any concern at all about taking judicial notice of matters which are under appeal, that could be resolved simply by removing the name "Mr. Tadic." The incidents themselves are not contested. Mr. Tadic isn't contesting the incidents. His contest relates to his participation and involvement. So removing his name would achieve that end. So in our submission, in any event, the Rule is not designed to deal with a situation where its operation is dependent upon whether or not an appeal is being filed or not. In our submission, the Tadic decision is a final decision. It clearly comes within Rule 94, and Your Honours are in a position to take judicial notice of those matters. Now may not be the time when Your Honours have reached the point where you should take judicial notice of these matters. But in my submission, Your Honours, the time will be reached when traversing all of these matters in each case will become so onerous and so unnecessary that the point will have been reached when judicial notice of all these things should be taken having regard to the expediency of the trial. In my submission, the time is now. They're extensively canvassed in the Tadic case. Clearly the Trial Chamber regarded them as relevant and important, because they included them in their judgement. Clearly, in relation to all of those matters, there's no major controversy which touches directly upon the accused themselves, general events in relation to the vast majority of them, which are pleaded and which are required, in our submission, for the purposes of establishing that the widespread and systematic nature of the crime, motive, and other general matters, that they could easily be taken judicial notice of and incorporated. But at the end of the day, it's a matter for Your Honours. It's for you to decide what you want to take judicial notice of, and we can only assist you, in what way we can, in drawing your attention to matters which we consider you can safely take judicial notice of. Unless I can assist, Your Honour, that's my submission on that particular motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann. Would anybody for the Defence like to say anything? I see Mr. Fila, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honour, I appreciate your efforts and also the efforts of my colleague Niemann, and I appreciate his point that we will in time reach that level. But there are two issues arising from this. In Tadic, if on appeal the judgement is either overturned or if the appeal of Mr. Niemann is upheld, the Tadic decision will change. Second, I don't understand the position. If you say that this was an internal armed conflict, because nobody questions that, what does Omarska have to do with Kosovo, with Milosevic, with the events in Vojvodina? This is the territory of another state, events which took place after Omarska and which were in another state. I, for instance, don't know why I would in a similar way ask some facts about the history of the state of Texas. But if we at some point come to the point where we -- crimes which may have taken place in the Kosovo indictment, we may then be able to use some of the facts here. But there are also other things that refer to Mr. Radic, and that is according to 421 and 422. These are not general facts which would point that Mladjo Radic committed a rape. If this is an adjudicated fact, then I don't know if there are any other -- what are we doing here? So this is wrong. In the case of Dokmanovic, we had worked with the Prosecution to stipulate a number of matters, and that is the only appropriate manner. But I cannot agree to link Kosovo here and to adjudicate that Mladjo Radic committed a crime. If that is what we agree on, then what is it that we do not agree on? So the position that we take is that we have to only take into account the cases which have been fully completed and on which we can base our agreements. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does anybody else want to say anything? The next motion that I have is the request by the Prosecution for the admission of documentary evidence. The Defence position, as I understand it, in relation to these documents, is that there is a dispute about a video, 41, "Victims of War, Time to Mourn," as there's no transcript as yet available. But that apart, I understand there to be no dispute about the admission of these documents. I would say the fact that a document is admitted does not mean, of course, that the Trial Chamber in any way attributes weight to it, if any. It is merely part of the evidence, and when the Trial Chamber comes to consider all the evidence, it will have to determine what weight, if any, a particular document is afforded. At this stage, Pre-Trial admission merely allows the Prosecution to produce the document. I would also add this: That it would not preclude in any way, in my judgement, anybody objecting to a particular document if some matter arose which in their view made the document inadmissible. I would not see it as precluding any further debate as to admissibility but merely admitting it at this stage. If that represents the Defence position, then the motion could be allowed, except in relation to this video, which would obviously require rather more attention, and that could be given in the next few months before the trial. Perhaps someone could tell me if that does represent the Defence position.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, that precisely represents the Defence position. Let me clarify videotape 411. First of all, because they are victims that are speaking, and so their testimony would become evidence, so to speak; second, the tape was taped in the German language, and German is not a language which we speak; neither is it the official language of the Tribunal. So the Defence suggested that, if the Prosecution insists on having this tape, that a transcript be made or that it be translated into English, and then we can see what it's about. Therefore the position of the Defence is just as you have explained it and interpreted it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Can we deal, then, with the tape. I can't remember -- I've got 41, but it may be 411.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My understanding, it's 41, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In relation to that, Your Honours, yes, we take the point, and we will endeavour to make a translation available for that, and we can take that up as a separate matter. So it does resolve all matters except one question, Your Honour, and that is that in the motions, the Defence have said that among the challenges they wish to reserve the right to -- and we don't quarrel with this -- they wish to reserve the right to authenticity. Now, I think that what I say with authenticity and relevance, I think relevance will be dealt with anyway. The question of authenticity does raise this issue: If we don't know about which documents they are going to contest the authenticity of, it is unlikely that we will call the evidence in our case in chief, as such, because there is no point in doing it merely on the basis of suspecting which ones -- we won't know which documents they're going to challenge, in terms of authenticity. It seems to us that if they could tell us in advance, we can then cater for that in our case in chief by calling appropriate evidence to deal with authenticity. Alternatively, so long as it's a matter that everybody's in agreement with, we would be quite as happy to deal with it by way of rebuttal, so that if in the course of the trial, in the course of both the Prosecution and the Defence case, it emerges that a document or a number of documents are challenged on the basis of authenticity, then we could deal with that in the rebuttal case.
