In my submission, that would be the most efficient way, because it would, a) save the Defence the burden of now having to determine which ones they wish to challenge the authenticity of, because they may in fact change their mind, in the course of the trial, on this question. Secondly, it's possible that at the end of the case, when it comes to the rebuttal case, we ourselves may say, "Well, look, we're not going to proceed with that," and for the sake of expediency not proceed to establish the authenticity and therefore withdraw it. We can do it that way. It seems to me to be much more efficient to allow the Prosecution, on everybody's understanding that we will have the opportunity to address authenticity at the rebuttal stage, and if everybody is in agreement with that, then that would be the way that I think it could be most efficiently disposed of. But if Your Honour wishes to deal with it in our case in chief, we are very happy to do that, but we need to know which ones are going to be challenged on that basis. So that would necessitate an order from Your Honours directing the Defence to inform us which ones are challenged on the basis of authenticity. If we proceed down the route of dealing with it in rebuttal, no order would be necessary, because we can pick that up in the course of the case, and we will know, by the time we get to the rebuttal case, what ones are challenged on authenticity and what aren't. That's the only matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does the Defence want to comment on that proposal?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The Defence quite simply saw the documents that it received from the Prosecution, and it seeks the right to deny the value of the documents when they are presented as evidence. They are presented as evidence; I cannot accept that they are absolutely authentic, and I would like to take advantage of the time to see whether they are authentic. If I ascertain that they are authentic or not, then I will do as has been suggested. But I have no reason to doubt the good intentions of the Prosecution, nor do I think that they have given us documents which are not authentic. This is just in case we feel, sometime along the line, that some document is not authentic. If we don't do this in any of the cases, then of course all the documents are relevant and authentic, and that is what Mr. Niemann has just said, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, I accept Mr. Fila's stance, and I would like to underline that we have understood that not all these documents may be used. They are documents, they are parts of press cuttings from the period of the indictment, and the question is; when they will occur with regard to individual facts? The Defence merely wish to state that when a document of this kind appears, it will give its opinions, and how far -- and its probative value and authenticity, perhaps. But we're not going to make the work of the Prosecution more difficult, because in the time that we have before us, we shall be seeing whether the documents are authentic or not, and we will of course present our views. So I don't see any contesting views there, and I don't see that we will have to give our views on every document. Every document will be assessed on its own merits, and of course if we feel that one is not authentic, we will say so. But I think that we actually agree and don't want to prolong the process any further. Thank you, Your Honours. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, as far as this motion is concerned, we shall order that the documents be admitted. If there is a dispute about authenticity, it can be raised at trial, and the Prosecution will be in the position of calling rebuttal evidence as they suggest. That seems to us a sensible and neat way of dealing with the matter. The remaining motion concerns expert evidence. The evidence in question is that of Dr. Hanne Greve, who gave evidence in Kovacevic and Tadic. The Defence position, as I understand it, is this: That at the moment they object to the admission of the evidence, largely because they want to cross-examine the witness, and they haven't had that possibility, or they wouldn't have that possibility if she were not called. Supposing this were the position -- and I merely put it forward as a suggestion: That the transcripts which the Prosecution refer to, together with the exhibits, be admitted as evidence in chief of the witness; so that means that the witness would not have to go through it all again, having given it on previous occasions at the behest of the Prosecution, but that she be brought here for cross-examination so that these accused may have the opportunity of cross-examining her during the trial. Is that a solution which seems practicable?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, Your Honours. That is the position of the Defence. We agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does the Prosecution want to say anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honour, yes. I think perhaps what Your Honour has suggested is the best solution to the matter, and I think we are very content with that, with two possible issues that I might raise. One, again, the question of authenticity has been raised with relation to the documents that she tenders. It may be that it's not quite the same issue, because she can deal with authenticity to some extent herself; but in relation to some of the documents, she may not able to deal with them, so we merely ask that we be extended the opportunity to deal with authenticity in the rebuttal case should that become necessary. It may not become necessary at all, because we'll have a witness here dealing with the documents, and it may not even raise itself. The other point I wish to raise, Your Honour, is that at this stage, I don't think there are any other matters that we would wish to ask her in chief which are separate and distinct from what she has already testified to in both the case of Tadic and Kovacevic, but it's possible we may want to raise fresh matters which she hasn't touched upon. In that event, Your Honours, we would just intimate at this stage that we would like to make an application at the relevant time should that become necessary. Finally, Your Honours, I just remind Your Honours of the recent decision in Aleksovski, where this document in fact could be tendered as a hearsay statement. I don't wish to pursue it any further than just to remind Your Honours of that. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Aleksovski may not be appropriate in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It may not be, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But if, therefore, the Prosecutor could examine, with leave, that would presumably satisfy your requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it just occurred to me, before I sit down, may we treat the transcripts in both those cases as her statement, rather than having the trouble of going to her and obtaining from her a statement? I seek to do that. She has now been appointed a judge of the European Court of Human Rights, and she's very busy, and we don't wish to trouble her with that if we can possibly avoid having to obtain another statement. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The transcripts and exhibits of the witness will be admitted as evidence in chief, but the witness must be available for cross-examination, the Prosecution to have leave to examine in chief, only with leave, the statements, the transcripts, rather, of the evidence of the witness, are to be treated as her statement. So there will be no further statement from the witness, simply those transcripts, which should clearly cover that particular aspect of the case. We will consider the motion, the application in relation to judicial notice of adjudicated facts, and we will give our decision on that in due course. Now, unless there are any other matters to be dealt with in open session, I propose that we go to closed session for a Status Conference. Are there any other matters which anybody would like to raise in open Court? Very well, we'll go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Status Conference, at 12.44. 22 23 24 25
